title: Just a little hoarse
objective: Recognize inhalation injury and airway burns that need early airway protection
secondaryObjectives: Assess a burn: airway and inhalation injury first, then size by percentage of body surface and depth

brief.situation: 02:15 in the emergency department. You are the nurse in a resuscitation room. Mr. Petrov, 45, was pulled from a bedroom fire. He has burns to his face and forearms and says he 'feels fine apart from the hands'.
handover: Triage: ESI 2. Heart rate 110, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99% on a non-rebreather, blood pressure 138/84. Soot around the nose and mouth.

The department's burn standing order: high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather, two large-bore IVs, a carboxyhemoglobin level, burns covered with clean film, and the physician called at once for any sign of airway injury.
The emergency physician and the anesthesia team are in the department.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and treat as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

Hoarse voice; singed nasal hairs; soot in the mouth; black flecks in his sputum; no stridor yet.

A harsh noise starts on each breath in. Mr. Petrov looks frightened.

why.question: Mr. Petrov now has a noise on breathing in. What does it mean, and what do you do?

parts.label: What it means
parts.criteria: Enclosed space, soot, singed hairs and hoarseness are inhalation injury; new stridor means swelling is narrowing the airway and will get worse over hours.
parts.modelAnswer: This is an inhalation injury: closed room, soot, singed hairs and a hoarse voice. The stridor means the airway is swelling shut, and it will get worse.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Physician and anesthesia now for early intubation; keep him upright on high-flow oxygen; no CT or transfer first; hand off.
parts.modelAnswer: Get the physician and anesthesia now to secure the airway early, keep him sitting up on high-flow oxygen, and don't send him anywhere first.

noProgress.rationale: A burned airway still unprotected an hour on is harm here.

expertPath.text: High-flow oxygen, two IVs, sit up.
Airway exam: hoarse, soot, singed hairs. Reassess.
Physician and anesthesia now; hand off.

unsafe.headline: A burned airway sent to CT
unsafe.body: A patient whose airway may close stays where it can be secured, sitting up. Imaging waits.

worsened.headline: Airway closed
worsened.body: Hoarseness after an enclosed-space fire is a warning. Stridor means the swelling is advancing; early intubation is easier than late.

wrongRoute.headline: To the ward
wrongRoute.body: A hoarse voice after smoke in a closed room does not wait until morning.

target.headline: Airway secured early
target.body: You looked in the mouth, listened to the voice, reassessed and called at the first stridor. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: Airway secured, with delays
recovered.body: Check how long the stridor went before the call.

time_up.headline: Still unprotected
time_up.body: Airway swelling after smoke inhalation can progress over hours, then suddenly.

scoring.modelReasoning: A fire in a closed room, soot, singed nasal hairs, black sputum and a hoarse voice point to inhalation injury even when the saturation looks fine. High-flow oxygen, access and sitting up come first, and he is reassessed often. When stridor appears the airway is closing: the physician and anesthesia secure it early, before swelling makes it impossible.

sigQ.ask: While you assess: which finding raises suspicion of inhalation injury most?

choices.label: A hoarse voice after a fire in a closed room

sigQ.explain: Hoarse voice, stridor, carbonaceous sputum, singed nasal or facial hair and burns in an enclosed space raise suspicion of airway injury.

whyQ.ask: While the team takes over: why secure the airway early in inhalation injury?

choices.label: Swelling can progress over hours and close the airway

whyQ.explain: Airway compromise can develop over hours and may only come to light in crisis; early intubation prevents trouble with further swelling.
